passages.t: Michael rises, and the dead will awake
passages.happening:
‘At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up’ (verse 1). There will be a time of distress like none since nations began. But at that time Daniel's people, everyone whose name is found written in the book, will be delivered.

‘And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt’ (verse 2). ‘Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever’ (verse 3).

The messenger tells Daniel to shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. ‘Many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
This chapter completes the final vision and closes the book. Chapter 11 ended with a persecuting king who magnifies himself and falls. The question left open is what becomes of those who died faithful under him, the wise who fell by sword and flame. Chapter 12 answers: death will not have the last word.

Verse 2 is the clearest statement in the Old Testament that the dead will rise bodily. Sleeping in the dust is a picture of death, and waking is a picture of resurrection. On the critical dating, the chapter was written for Jews suffering under Antiochus IV between 167 and 164 BC, and the promise answered their most painful question: whether those who died for the law had lost everything. The same hope appears in 2 Maccabees 7, where a mother and her seven sons die under torture trusting that God will raise them. On the traditional dating, the chapter was revealed to Daniel about 536 BC as a promise for the crisis to come and for the end of history.

The book written in heaven is a picture of God's knowledge of his own people. The wise of verse 3 are the maskilim of chapter 11, those with insight who taught many and paid for it. They will shine like the stars.

To seal a book was to close it up and keep it safe until the right time. The vision was not for idle reading but for a time that was coming.
passages.later: Isaiah had sung the same hope: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!” (Isaiah 26:19). Jesus spoke of the same two destinies: ‘all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out’ (John 5:28-29). And he said, ‘Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father’ (Matthew 13:43).
passages.hard:
Does many who sleep mean that only some will be raised?

Verse 2 says many who sleep in the dust will awake, not all. Some interpreters take that at face value as a limited resurrection: in its setting, the persecution of chapter 11 produced both martyrs and traitors, and God raises the faithful to vindicate them and the traitors to judge them. On this view Daniel is not yet teaching a resurrection of all humanity, which later revelation makes plain.

Others note that many in Hebrew can carry an inclusive sense, the many as against the few, and that the verse describes two groups that together cover everyone. Jesus' words in John 5:28-29, which speak of all who are in the graves and the same two destinies, suggest that he read Daniel as describing the resurrection of all.

Either way, the chapter is clear on its main points: the dead will be raised bodily, the resurrection leads to two different ends, and the faithful who died under persecution will be vindicated. Christians confess the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting as first-order truths. How much Daniel 12 by itself teaches about their scope is a question on which careful readers differ. These notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person.
passages.asks: The wise who taught many and fell are promised that they will shine. Ask whose faithfulness you have seen go unrewarded in this life. And ask how the promise of resurrection changes what you are willing to risk for what is right.

passages.t: How long? Go on your way, Daniel
passages.happening:
Daniel sees two others, one on each bank of the river (verse 5). One asks the man dressed in linen, who is above the waters, ‘How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?’ (verse 6).

The man in linen raises both hands toward heaven and swears by him who lives forever: ‘It will be for a time, and times, and half a time’ (verse 7). When the power of the holy people has finally been shattered, all these things will be completed.

‘I heard, but I did not understand’ (verse 8). So Daniel asks, ‘My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?’ (verse 8).

The answer is gentle and firm: ‘Go on your way, Daniel’ (verse 9), for the words are sealed until the time of the end. ‘Many will be purified, made spotless, and refined, but the wicked will continue to act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The question How long has been asked before in this book, by the holy ones in chapter 8. The answer is the same span as chapter 7: a time, and times, and half a time, usually taken as three and a half, half of seven, a time of trouble that is real but broken off.

The man raises both hands to swear, a doubled oath, by the one who lives forever. Whatever the length of the trouble, its end is sworn by God's own life.

Daniel's honesty in verse 8 is worth noticing. He has received more visions than anyone in the book, and he says he does not understand. He asks for the outcome and is told to go his way. The first hearers were not given a timetable either. They were given a promise, a call to faithfulness, and the assurance that the wise would understand what they needed when they needed it.
passages.later: The same span returns in Revelation for the church under pressure: the woman is nourished ‘for a time, and times, and half a time’ (Revelation 12:14). And at the end of Revelation the seer is told the opposite of Daniel: ‘Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near’ (Revelation 22:10).
passages.asks: Daniel admitted that he did not understand, and he was told to go on his way. Ask whether you can live faithfully with what you do not understand. And ask what it would mean to trust a promise sworn by the one who lives forever.

passages.happening:
‘And from the time the daily sacrifice is abolished and the abomination of desolation set up, there will be 1,290 days’ (verse 11). ‘Blessed is he who waits and reaches the end of the 1,335 days’ (verse 12).

And the last word to Daniel: ‘But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The 1,290 and 1,335 days are both a little more than three and a half years. Critical scholars often suggest they reflect later adjustments as the end was awaited, or that they are symbolic figures. Those who apply them to the Maccabean period note that the temple was rededicated in December 164 BC, about three years after its desecration. Futurist interpreters see the extra days as periods after a future time of trouble. Many interpreters of every view hold that the numbers give not a timetable but the assurance that the suffering has a fixed limit, known to God.

The book that began with young Daniel taken captive to Babylon ends with old Daniel told to go his way and rest, with a promise that he too will rise. He will not see the end of the visions in his own life. He is promised his inheritance at the end of the days.

The first hearers, some of whom would die before the trouble ended, were given the same promise. The last word of the book is not a date. It is rest, and rising.
passages.later: Isaiah promises that ‘the earth will bring forth her dead’ (Isaiah 26:19). And Revelation shows the dead before the throne, where ‘there were open books, and one of them was the Book of Life’ (Revelation 20:12).
passages.hard:
Do the 1,290 and 1,335 days give a date for the end?

No, and these notes calculate none. The numbers have been read in several ways, and none of them has proved a key to dating the end. The history of attempts to calculate the end from Daniel's numbers is long, and every date set has passed. Jesus said, ‘No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father’ (Matthew 24:36).

The verse itself points the reader elsewhere, to the one ‘who waits and reaches the end’ (verse 12). And to Daniel, who wanted to know the outcome, the answer was not a date but a promise: you will rest, and you will rise.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The last word to Daniel is rest, and rise. Ask what it would mean for you to go your way until the end, faithful in ordinary days. And ask whether the hope of rising to your inheritance is a real comfort to you, or only words.
